title: Ganesh Chaturthi: welcoming Ganesha home
hook: clay Ganeshas are carried home with drums, kept for days, then given back to the water
carry: welcome it, then let it go

segments.voice: Last time: Janmashtami, a baby carried out of a prison through a flood at midnight. Your line was the good arrives at midnight. Did you sit in the dark for one breath? Day seventy-nine.

Picture the streets of a city in Maharashtra at the end of summer. Drums so loud you feel them in your chest. Families walking home carrying a Ganesha made of clay, some small enough to hold in two hands, some so huge they ride on trucks, trunk and belly and all. Children shouting a name. You met this god back at the start of the stories camp: the boy at the door, the elephant head, the broken tusk, the mouse, the sweets. Today, the festival where he comes to stay. For a few days. And then, on purpose, everyone lets him go.
screen: `DRUMS IN THE STREETS.` → `A CLAY GANESHA CARRIED HOME.` → `HE STAYS, THEN GOES.`

segments.voice: Ganesh Chaturthi. Chaturthi means the fourth: the fourth day of the moon's bright half, in the late-summer month of Bhadrapada, the day tradition celebrates as Ganesha's birthday. Here's how it goes in many homes. You bring the clay image in, and a priest or a family elder invites Ganesha to be present in it, as a guest. For the next days he's treated like the most honored visitor you've ever had. Lamps morning and evening. Flowers. Blades of durva grass, which he loves. And modaks, the sweet dumplings, the same sweets you met as prasad weeks ago, the offering that comes back. Friends come to visit him. Then, after a day and a half, or three, five, seven, or ten days, depending on the family, comes the hardest part. The family carries him to the sea, a river, a lake, or a tank of water, with drums and dancing, and gently gives him back. The clay melts. The crowds call out Ganpati Bappa Morya, and then a second line in Marathi that means: come back soon next year. For centuries it was mostly a home festival. In 1893, in Pune, the leader Bal Gangadhar Tilak helped turn it into a great public celebration, and the huge street festivals grew from there. Why melt him? Many teachers explain it like this: the clay comes from the earth and returns to it. The form was for us, so we could welcome something we can't see, and letting it go says the god was never trapped in the clay. It's also a rehearsal. Everything we love, we welcome and one day let go. The festival makes that joyful.
screen: `CHATURTHI: THE FOURTH DAY.` · `AN HONORED GUEST, WITH MODAKS.` · `GIVEN BACK TO THE WATER.` · `WELCOMED, THEN LET GO, WITH JOY.`

segments.voice: Hold something small in your hands. A cup, a stone, a ring, anything you like. Feel its weight. Think of what it means to you, or what it reminds you of. Welcome it, the way a family welcomes Ganesha: really look at it, really be glad it's here. Now, slowly, set it down in front of you. Open your hands. Notice what it feels like to let go of something you love, gently, without dropping it. Stay with your open hands for the rest of the sit. The bell holds the time.
Ganesh Chaturthi. The fourth day, when Ganesha is welcomed home in clay, honored for days, and given back to the water.
Your line: welcome it, then let it go. Today, enjoy one good thing fully, a meal, a visit, a moment, and let it end without grabbing. Day seventy-nine.

howItsDone: For Ganesh Chaturthi, Hindu families and neighborhoods install clay images of Ganesha at home or in public pandals, worship him with lamps, flowers, durva grass and modaks for one and a half to ten days, then immerse the image in water in a joyful procession; many now choose unpainted clay or eco-friendly images.

what a scholar hears: the rite invites the god into the image and later releases him; the public festival owes much to Tilak's Pune in 1893.

notes: Festival buffer day; the review picks up day 78.
Date: shukla chaturthi of Bhadrapada; confirm.
Installation (prana pratishtha) and release are described without Sanskrit terms ('invites Ganesha to be present... as a guest'); confirm.
The meaning of immersion is attributed to 'many teachers'; confirm.
'Ganpati Bappa Morya' and the Marathi 'pudhchya varshi lavkar ya' (come soon next year) paraphrased; confirm.
Tilak 1893 Pune: widely cited; confirm. Some histories credit Bhausaheb Rangari's public Ganpati in Pune a year earlier; the script's 'helped turn it' allows for that.
Audit (10% sample, 2026-09-30): the teach read as if 'Ganpati Bappa Morya' itself meant 'come back soon next year'. Reworded so the Marathi farewell is a second line (pudhchya varshi lavkar ya).
